claims.text: Incorporating multiple refractory elements into equimolar WTaTiVZr produces a refined, chemically homogeneous microstructure.
Equimolar WTaTiVZr contains stable nanoscale Zr/Ti-rich precipitates at grain boundaries.
The refined microstructure and grain-boundary precipitates enable more efficient dislocation nucleation.
The refined microstructure and grain-boundary precipitates enable more efficient dislocation motion.
The proposed microstructural features promote dynamic grain-boundary sliding at high temperature.
The proposed dislocation and grain-boundary mechanisms enhance plastic strain and toughness relative to pure tungsten.
The tested WTaTiVZr alloy has a uniform, fine-grained microstructure with dispersed nanoscale precipitates.
Commercially processed pure tungsten has coarse grains.
Commercially processed pure tungsten has limited secondary-phase dispersions.
The high-entropy composition stabilizes a uniform, fine-grained matrix with distributed precipitates.
The distributed precipitates act as dislocation sources.
The distributed precipitates also act as barriers to dislocation motion.
The dual source-and-barrier role of the precipitates enhances elevated-temperature dislocation mobility.
The proposed microstructure facilitates grain-boundary sliding without premature crack initiation.
At 1200–1400°C, WTaTiVZr should sustain a higher plastic strain before failure than pure tungsten.
At 1200–1400°C, WTaTiVZr should absorb more mechanical energy before failure than pure tungsten.
The hypothesized advantage should apply primarily at approximately 1200–1400°C under tensile or creep loading.
At substantially lower temperatures or under non-creep-dominated deformation, the proposed microstructural advantages may not manifest to the same extent.
Analogous behavior has been observed in similar refractory high-entropy alloys.
